content: 1. Pre-introduction assessments were conducted at national, regional, and district or county levels to evaluate readiness for the malaria vaccine rollout. 2. Post-introduction supportive supervision was implemented to ensure the smooth integration of the vaccine into existing health systems. 3. Review meetings were held at health facility levels to validate and reconcile Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) data. 4. Supportive supervision was carried out by national, regional, and district or county health authorities to monitor and improve vaccine delivery. 5. Mapping of unimmunized and under-immunized children was conducted to identify gaps in vaccine coverage, following WHO guidelines. 6. Communication strategies included the development, validation, pre-testing, and translation of information, education, and communication materials. 7. Communication materials and field guides were printed and distributed to support vaccine awareness campaigns. 8. Public awareness efforts included press releases in newspapers, announcements via public address systems, and broadcasting messages on radio stations, community centers, and mobile vans. 9. Spokesperson training sessions were conducted to ensure accurate and consistent messaging about the vaccine. 10. Planning meetings were held to coordinate vaccine introduction activities. 11. Social mobilization activities, such as peer education, orientation sessions, social announcements, and periodic intensification of routine immunization, were carried out to engage communities. 12. Sensitization efforts targeted district health management teams, community leaders, religious leaders, community health assistants, volunteers, and households through door-to-door approaches. 13. National and/or regional-level launch events were organized to mark the first administration of the malaria vaccine. 14. Stakeholder engagements were conducted at national, regional, and district or county levels to ensure alignment and support for the vaccine introduction. 15. Vaccine uptake was equitable across sex and socioeconomic groups, with no negative impact on the uptake of other childhood vaccinations, insecticide-treated net (ITN) use, or health-seeking behavior for febrile illnesses. 16. The introduction of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine extended the reach of malaria prevention tools. In the three pilot countries, over two-thirds of children who did not sleep under an ITN received at least their first dose of the malaria vaccine. 17. The vaccine introduction increased access to malaria prevention tools (ITNs or RTS,S/AS01) to over 90% of children in each of the three pilot countries. 18. Evidence supporting these findings is detailed in the unpublished full evidence report on the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine background paper, particularly in Section 10 on equity considerations. 19. Further details on equity are also included in the SAGE/MPAG Evidence-to-Recommendations framework. 20. The RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine was deemed acceptable by the target population, including eligible children and their caregivers, based on administrative data, household surveys, and qualitative studies showing high acceptance and desirability. 21. Key stakeholders, including ministries of health and immunization program managers, also found the vaccine acceptable, as evidenced by post-introduction evaluations and interviews with health providers. 22. Household surveys indicated no reduction in ITN use in areas where the vaccine was introduced, demonstrating that the vaccine did not displace other malaria prevention measures. 23. Health-seeking behavior for febrile illnesses remained consistent between intervention and comparison groups. 24. The WHO framework for recommending the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine, endorsed by SAGE and MPAG in 2019, emphasized the importance of making recommendations as soon as the vaccine's risk-benefit profile was established with confidence. 25. The framework clarified that high coverage, including with the fourth vaccine dose, should not be a prerequisite for recommendation, as data showed benefits from three or four doses in areas of moderate to high malaria transmission. 26. The RTS,S/AS01 vaccine is considered safe and well-tolerated, with a small risk of febrile seizures within seven days of vaccination, primarily within 2–3 days. 27. Proper planning and staff training for pharmacovigilance are essential before vaccine introduction. 28. The vaccine demonstrated the ability to achieve high coverage and impact quickly when delivered through routine immunization systems, with a 30% reduction in severe malaria observed in areas with widespread ITN use and good access to diagnosis and treatment. 29. Modeling studies indicate that the vaccine is cost-effective in areas of moderate to high malaria transmission. 30. The RTS,S/AS01 vaccine increases access to malaria prevention without negatively affecting the uptake of other childhood vaccinations, ITN use, or health-seeking behavior for febrile illnesses. 31. The feasibility of vaccine introduction was demonstrated through good and equitable coverage achieved via routine immunization systems, even during the COVID-19 pandemic. 32. Across the three pilot countries, 7 million RTS,S/AS01 vaccine doses were administered, and more than 650,000 children received their first dose. 33. All three countries reached over 70% of their target populations with the first RTS,S/AS01 dose and at least 62% with the third dose. 34. Further details on feasibility are included in the SAGE/MPAG Evidence-to-Recommendations framework. 35. Malaria case management, including early diagnosis and prompt, effective treatment, remains a cornerstone of malaria control and elimination strategies. 36. The WHO Guidelines for the Treatment of Malaria, first developed in 2006 and revised periodically, provide recommendations on clinical practice and public health policy to achieve optimal health outcomes. 37. The third edition of the guidelines consolidates updated recommendations based on new evidence, particularly regarding dosing in children and the use of drugs to prevent malaria in high-risk groups. 38. Since 2006, countries where Plasmodium falciparum malaria is endemic have progressively updated their treatment policies from monotherapy to the currently recommended artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs). 39. ACTs are highly effective and well-tolerated, contributing significantly to reductions in global malaria morbidity and mortality. 40. However, resistance to artemisinins has recently emerged in Southeast Asia, threatening these gains. 41. Core principles for malaria treatment include early diagnosis and prompt, effective treatment to prevent progression to severe disease, rational use of antimalarial agents to limit drug resistance, and adherence to full treatment courses. 42. Universal access to parasitological diagnosis is now possible with quality-assured rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), which are suitable for use in primary health care and community settings. 43. Combination therapy, involving at least two effective antimalarial drugs with different mechanisms of action, is essential to prevent or delay resistance and ensure treatment success. 44. Weight-based dosing is critical to ensure optimal drug concentrations for effective treatment and to minimize transmission. 45. Malaria diagnosis should focus on identifying true cases to guide rational use of antimalarial medicines. Clinical diagnosis alone has low specificity and often leads to overtreatment. 46. Parasitological diagnosis should be confirmed with microscopy or RDTs, supported by quality assurance programs. 47. Antimalarial treatment should be limited to cases with positive test results, and patients with negative results should be reassessed for other causes of fever. 48. In cases of suspected severe malaria, immediate antimalarial treatment should not be delayed, even in the absence of parasitological confirmation. 49. Microscopy and RDTs are the primary methods for malaria diagnosis, with RDTs being particularly useful in settings without access to quality-assured microscopy. 50. If initial blood film examination is negative in patients with severe malaria symptoms, repeated testing or RDTs should be performed. If all tests are negative, other causes of illness should be investigated and treated.
